extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, legal counsel, and juvenile justice facility administrators
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX compliance — retaliation and appearance codes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards interpreting Title IX provisions on sex-differentiated appearance codes, juvenile justice facility placements, burden on schools, and the prohibition and definition of retaliation (§§106.2, 106.31, 106.44, 106.45, 106.71). Useful for institutions and administrators implementing or defending Title IX policies and for those assessing complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of sex-differentiated appearance codes subject to Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts (including Peltier) have affirmed that a recipient's enforcement of a sex-differentiated appearance code is subject to Title IX's statutory prohibition on sex discrimination; different hair length or dress requirements for boys and girls fall within Title IX scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient is barred from carrying out different treatment or separation in a manner that subjects 'any person' to more than de minimis harm, except as permitted by Title IX. It is not a defense to point to a 'comparably burdensome' requirement for other students or to argue 'equal burdens' — discriminating against members of both sexes does not eliminate liability (see Bostock; Peltier). The Department disagrees with courts that apply a 'comparable burdens' test and retains that sex-specific appearance requirements may violate Title IX if they harm individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of §106.31(a)(2) and living-facility exception
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) does not apply in contexts where different treatment that causes more than de minimis harm is 'otherwise permitted under Title IX,' including in 'living facilities' (20 U.S.C. 1686). The Department's Title IX regulations apply to juvenile justice facilities only to the extent they receive Federal funds and only to education programs or activities offered by such facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juvenile justice facilities retain obligations to protect their populations. Placement or treatment decisions in living facilities may be analyzed under exceptions in Title IX; generalized anecdotal data alleging increased risk of sexual assault do not, by themselves, justify departing from the regulatory approach. Recipients must consider applicable PREA obligations but PREA references do not automatically permit sex-based placements that conflict with Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of burdens on schools (Regulatory Impact Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters asserted that §106.31(a)(2) would impose costs (facility retrofits, administrative/legal costs, monitoring, training) and could push recipients to forego federal student aid programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department's Regulatory Impact Analysis addresses costs and benefits associated with the final regulations, including those specifically attributable to §106.31(a)(2). Claims about burdens will be weighed in that analysis; however, asserted burdens do not automatically override nondiscrimination obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of retaliation — required motive for coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Retaliation is prohibited when an adverse action is taken 'for the purpose of interfering' with any right or privilege secured by Title IX or 'because' the person participated in the Title IX process (per §106.2 and §106.71). The Supreme Court in Jackson recognizes retaliation for complaining of sex discrimination as 'discrimination' on the basis of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition limits coverage to actions motivated by interference with Title IX rights or by participation; it does not cover adverse actions unrelated to sex. Determination requires establishing motive or causation consistent with the interference and participation clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-complaints and defense submissions do not automatically constitute retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent may file a cross-complaint, and a recipient may consolidate complaints under §106.45(e); a cross-complaint will not constitute retaliation if there is another legitimate reason for the cross-complaint that is not a pretext for sex-based retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should allow consolidation where appropriate and must evaluate whether a cross-complaint is a genuine claim or a pretextual attempt to retaliate. The regulations recognize the right to defend oneself while guarding against retaliatory misuse of cross-complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplining for false statements (§106.45(h)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations prohibit disciplining a party, witness, or others participating in a grievance procedure for making a false statement based solely on the recipient's determination whether sex discrimination occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion to discipline for false statements where there is evidence other than, or in addition to, the outcome of the Title IX proceeding. Relying solely on a finding that sex discrimination did not occur to conclude statements were false is impermissible because it can chill reporting and conflates distinct determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation analysis framework (adverse action, knowledge, causation, legitimate reason, pretext)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether specific conduct constitutes retaliation requires a close examination of all facts and circumstances: whether the action was adverse, whether the recipient knew of the protected activity, whether there is a causal connection, and whether the recipient had a legitimate, non-retaliatory reason (or the action is pretextual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: disciplining a student seeking pregnancy-related reasonable modifications would generally be an adverse action; OCR must determine knowledge and causation and then evaluate the genuineness of the stated reason. Trauma-related misconduct by a complainant may not be disciplined if the motive is to interfere with Title IX rights. Consider whether exceptions (e.g., religious exemption) apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of regulatory examples but retention of policy (placement of examples in preamble)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department removed certain illustrative examples from the text of §106.71 (including the proposed example about charging code of conduct violations and a peer-retaliation example) and placed discussion of examples in the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal from the regulatory text does not represent a substantive policy change; the Department prefers to discuss non-exhaustive examples in the preamble so that regulatory text remains focused on standards rather than illustrative lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amnesty policies are discretionary and Title IX Coordinators must monitor barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may adopt broader amnesty policies under which they will not discipline students for collateral conduct related to an incident of sex-based harassment; however, Title IX does not require all recipients to adopt such policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under §106.44(b), Title IX Coordinators must monitor for potential barriers to reporting (e.g., fear of alcohol-related discipline) and take steps reasonably calculated to address such barriers; adopting amnesty policies is one approach recipients may consider when the Coordinator identifies such barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protections maintained in retaliation context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department enforces Title IX consistent with First Amendment requirements; merely criticizing a recipient's Title IX policies, practices, or an individual's participation in a grievance procedure generally would not alone constitute retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal of an explicit statement that 'exercise of First Amendment rights is not a form of retaliation' from §106.71 is not a substantive change; §106.6(d) and case law continue to protect speech and association. Whether exclusion or criticism constitutes retaliation depends on facts and whether the action was for the purpose of interfering with Title IX rights or because of participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a retaliation complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person specified in §106.45(a)(2) may make a retaliation complaint, which includes a complainant; a parent, guardian, or authorized legal representative; the Title IX Coordinator after making specified determinations; or any student, employee, or other person who was participating or attempting to participate in the recipient's education program or activity at the time of the alleged retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone who participated in any way in the Title IX process (complainant, respondent, witness) may file a retaliation complaint if they believe an adverse action was taken against them because of participation. Persons who were not participants may still complain if they believe an action was taken to interfere with their Title IX rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient obligations when it 'has' information about possible retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised proposed §106.71 to require a response when a recipient 'has' information that reasonably may constitute retaliation under Title IX or this part (rather than only when it 'receives' such information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a recipient has such information, it is obligated to comply with §106.44, which includes offering and coordinating supportive measures, determining whether to initiate a complaint under certain circumstances, and taking prompt and effective steps to ensure sex discrimination does not continue or recur. The change clarifies that the recipient's duty is not limited to externally received reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution option for retaliation complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations clarify that a recipient may, as appropriate and consistent with §106.44(k), offer the parties to a retaliation complaint the option of an informal resolution process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal resolution may be used when appropriate and must comply with the procedural safeguards and requirements set out in §106.44(k). The availability of informal resolution does not alter the substantive prohibition on retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'retaliation' in §106.2: interference and participation clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.2 defines retaliation with an 'interference' clause (adverse action taken 'for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX') and a 'participation' clause (adverse action taken 'because' a person has reported, made a complaint, testified, assisted, or participated or refused to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under the Department's Title IX regulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These clauses are substantially similar to parallel clauses in the Title VI retaliation provision and delineate the two types of protected activity covered by the retaliation definition: actions taken to interfere with Title IX rights and actions taken in response to participation in Title IX processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may enforce codes of conduct for legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons; religious exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition on retaliation does not prevent a recipient from enforcing its code of conduct for legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons; furthermore, Title IX does not apply to an educational institution controlled by a religious organization to the extent application would be inconsistent with its religious tenets (20 U.S.C. 1681(a)(3); 34 CFR 106.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether disciplinary action constitutes retaliation, recipients and OCR must assess motive; enforcement that is genuine and nondiscriminatory is permitted. Religious exemptions remain available where statutory criteria are met.
